If I am unable to succeed,
what will you do?"
He replied,
"If I were a man of virtue, I would have a way.
But as I am a mere commoner,
I will clutch my ribs with my left hand, and bind my heart with my right,
standing until I starve and wither,
to proclaim to men of all directions:
'Yúhé was unable to bury his mother.'"
Yànzi said,
"Alright."
Thereupon, he went in to see the Duke,
He said:
"There was Féng of Hé,
his mother died, and the divination showed (the grave site) to be in the Lùqǐn (Roadside Palace),
right under the window? I wish to request (permission) to gather her bones (there)."
The Duke’s (Gōng) expression changed, and he was displeased,
saying:
"From ancient times until now,
have you ever heard of someone requesting to bury (someone) in the palace of a ruler?"
Yàn Zǐ replied, saying:
"The rulers of ancient times,
their palaces were moderate, not infringing on the dwellings of the living,
their terraces and pavilions were simple, not damaging the graves of the dead,
therefore, one never heard of anyone requesting to bury (someone) in the palace of a ruler.
Now, Your Lordship extravagantly builds palaces,
seizing the dwellings of the people,
extensively building terraces and pavilions,
damaging the graves of the people.
This causes the living to worry and be distressed,
unable to live in peace,
and the dead to be separated and displaced,
unable to have their bones gathered.
Abundant pleasures, extravagant travels,
and simultaneously being arrogant towards both life and death,
are not the conduct of a ruler.
Persisting in fulfilling desires,
without regard for the common people,
is not the way to survive.
Furthermore, I, Yīng, have heard that
The living cannot find peace,
call this accumulating worry;
the dead cannot be buried,
call this accumulating sorrow.
Those who accumulate worry resent,
those who accumulate sorrow are endangered,
it would be better for you, lord, to grant his request."
The Duke said:
"Agreed."
Yàn Zǐ withdrew, and Liángqiū Jù said:
"From ancient times until now,
I have never heard of anyone requesting burial in the ducal palace,
how could you grant this?"
The Duke said:
"To reduce people's dwellings,
to damage people's graves,
to insult people's funerals,
and to prohibit their burial,
is to show no kindness to the living,
and no respect to the dead.
The *Book of Poetry* says:
"While living, they dwell in separate rooms; when dead, they share the same grave."
How could I dare not grant it?"
Féng Yúhé then buried his mother beneath the window of the main palace,
removed his mourning clothes and hemp band,
wore plain clothes and straw sandals,
a black cap and purple leggings,
jumped but did not weep,
He prostrated himself but did not bow,
and then left weeping and sniveling.
2.21 *Duke Jǐng Gōng Mourns a Favored Concubine, Refusing Burial for Three Days; Yàn Zǐ Intervenes*
Duke Jǐng's favored concubine, Yīng Zǐ, died.
The Duke mourned for her,
not eating for three days,
his skin stuck to the mat, and he would not leave.
Those around him repeatedly advised,
but the Duke would not listen.
Yàn Zǐ entered and reported:
"A magician and a doctor together said:
'We heard that Yīng Zǐ died of illness
and wish to request to cure her.'"
The Duke was pleased and immediately rose,
saying:
"Can the illness still be remedied?"
Yàn Zǐ said:
"It is the way of the magician,
who considers himself a good doctor,
to request to try.
Please withdraw,
purify yourself with bathing, and eat and drink.
Vacate the palace of the sick one,
for they will also have matters involving ghosts and spirits."
The Duke said:
"Agreed."
He withdrew and bathed.
Yàn Zǐ ordered the coffin makers to proceed with the encoffining.
After the encoffining was complete, he said again:
"The doctor could not cure the illness,
and now the encoffining is done.
I dare not fail to report this."
The Duke changed his expression and was displeased,
and said:
"You, Master, use the doctor to instruct me,
and do not allow me to see,
about to encoffin and not report it to me,
that I am a ruler,
in name only."
Yàn Zǐ said:
"Does Your Lordship not know that the dead cannot be brought back to life?
I, Yīng, have heard that when the ruler is upright and the ministers follow, it is called obedience;
when the ruler is perverse and the ministers follow, it is called opposition.
Now Your Lordship does not follow the path of obedience but acts perversely,
those who follow wickedness are near,
those who speak of goodness are far away,
slander and flattery sprout and thrive,
while the worthy and good are abandoned and extinguished.
Therefore, flattery abounds in the lanes,
and wicked deeds fill the state.
In the past, my former lord, Duke Huán, employed Guǎn Zhòng and achieved hegemony,
favored Shù Diāo and was destroyed.
Now Your Lordship is thin on the rites for the worthy,
and thick on the grief for favored concubines.
Furthermore, ancient sage kings indulged personal feelings without harming conduct,
In preparing the dead for burial, do not lose affection;
in seeing off the dead, do not lose sorrow.
Excessive grief harms oneself;
loss of affection harms the living;
loss of sorrow harms one's nature.
Therefore, the sage kings regulated them.
Upon death, complete the burial preparations;
do not delay the affairs of the living;
coffins, outer coffins, clothing, and coverings should not harm the sustenance of the living;
weeping and dwelling in sorrow should not harm the way of the living.
Now you preserve a rotting corpse to linger with the living, extend affection to harm conduct,
follow sorrow to harm nature, this is your failing, my lord.
Therefore, the guests of the feudal lords are ashamed to enter our state;
the ministers of this court are ashamed to keep their posts;
exalting the ruler's conduct cannot guide the people;
following the ruler's desires cannot maintain the state.
Furthermore, Yīng has heard that
a corpse left to rot without preparation is called a disgraced corpse (lù shī),
and a stinking corpse left uncollected is called an exposed cadaver (chén zì).
To act contrary to the nature of enlightened rulers,
to conduct oneself in a way that invites the criticism of the people,
and to keep concubines among the
disgraced cadavers—this is unacceptable."
The Duke said:
"I was unaware;
please, instruct me on what to do, Master."
Yàn Zǐ replied again:
"The state's scholar-officials,
The lords, the four neighbors, and the guests are all outside,
Your Lordship should mourn him but with restraint."
Zhòng Ní heard this and said:
"The brightness of the stars
is not as good as the
dimness of the moon; the success of small matters
is not as good as the abandonment of great matters;
the errors of a gentleman
are better than the right of a petty man.
Could this be about Yàn Zǐ!"
2.22《Duke Jǐng Desires to Lavishly Bury Liángqiū Jù, Yàn Zǐ Advises Against It》
Liángqiū Jù died,
Duke Jǐng summoned Yàn Zǐ and told him,
saying:
"Jù was loyal and loved me,
I want to make his burial rich and generous,
and his tomb high and large."
Yàn Zǐ said:
"May I venture to ask, what are the manifestations of Jù's loyalty and love for you, my lord,
that I may hear them?"
The Duke said:
"I delight in playthings and good things,
but the officials were unable to provide them for me completely,
so Jù would supply me with his own possessions,
this is how I knew his loyalty;
whenever there was wind and rain, and I sought them at night, they were always available,
this is how I knew his love."
Yàn Zǐ said:
"If Yīng responds, it will be a crime;
if I don't respond, I will have no way to serve my lord. How dare I not respond!
Yīng has heard it said,
'A minister who monopolizes his ruler is called disloyal;
a son who monopolizes his father is called unfilial;
a wife who monopolizes her husband
is called (un)jealous.'
The way to serve a lord is to guide relatives towards father and elder brothers,
be courteous to all ministers,
be benevolent to the common people,
be trustworthy to the feudal lords, this is called loyalty.
The way to be a son is to love his brothers wholeheartedly,
extend (this love) to all uncles,
be kind and benevolent to all nephews and sons of brothers,
be sincere and trustworthy to friends, this is called filial piety.
The way to be a wife is
to make all the concubines joyful with their husband; this is called not being jealous.
Now, the people within the four borders are all your majesty's subjects,
and Wéi Jù only strives to love you.
Why is there a lack of those who love you?
The goods within the four borders all belong to your majesty,
yet Wéi Jù uses his private wealth to be loyal to you.
Why is there a scarcity of those who are loyal?
Jù's obstructing of the ministers
and blocking and misleading you, is that not excessive?'"
The Duke said,
"Excellent! Little one (Wēi Zǐ),
I didn't know Jù had gone this far."
Thereupon he stopped the work of building the mound.
He abolished the decree of lavish burials.
He ordered the officials to govern according to the law,
and for the ministers to present their faults and remonstrate.
Therefore, officials did not disregard the law,
ministers did not conceal their loyalty,
and the common people were greatly pleased.
2.23 *Jǐng Gōng yù yǐ rén lǐ zàng zǒu gǒu Yàn Zǐ jiàn* (Duke Jing wished to bury his hunting dog with the rites for humans, and Yan Zi remonstrated).
Duke Jǐng's hunting dog died.
The Duke ordered the outer court to prepare a coffin for it
and the inner court to provide offerings for it.
Yàn Zǐ heard of this
and remonstrated. The Duke said,
"It is merely a trivial thing,
I just wanted to give my attendants something to laugh about."
Yàn Zǐ said,
"You have erred, my lord!
To amass wealth without using it to benefit the people,
to discard valuables just to amuse your attendants,
to scorn the worries of the lowly people
and exalt the laughter of your attendants,
then there is no hope for the country.
Moreover, if the orphaned and elderly suffer from cold and hunger,
yet a dead dog receives offerings;
if widowers and widows are not cared for,
yet a dead dog receives a coffin,
conduct so perverse as this,
Bǎixìng wén zhī,
and will surely resent our lord.
The feudal lords will hear of this,
and will surely look down upon our state.
Resentment will gather among the common people,
and our power will be diminished in the eyes of the feudal lords,
and you then consider it a trivial matter,
Your Lordship should consider this."
The Duke said,
"Good."
He ordered the cooks to prepare a dog,
to entertain the assembled court officials.
2.24 《Duke Jǐng Keeps Three Brave Warriors Devoid of the Righteousness of Lord and Subject; Yànzǐ Advises》
Gōngsūn Jiē,
Tián Kāijiāng, and Gǔ Yězi served Duke Jǐng,
and were known for their bravery and strength in tiger-fighting.
Yànzǐ passed by and hurried (to show respect), but the three men did not rise.
Yànzǐ entered and saw the Duke, saying,
"Your servant has heard that a wise ruler, in employing brave and strong men,
(ensures) that above there is the righteousness of lord and subject, and below there is the principle of leadership and obedience.
Internally they can suppress violence, and externally they can intimidate enemies.
Above, (the ruler) benefits from their merits, and below, (the people) admire their courage,
therefore, their positions are honored and their stipends are substantial.
Now, Your Lordship's employment of brave and strong men
lacks the righteousness of lord and subject above,
and lacks the principle of leadership and obedience below.
"If internally they cannot suppress violence,
and externally they cannot intimidate enemies,
these are instruments of a state in peril,
better to remove them."
The Duke said:
"These three gentlemen,
to grapple them, I fear I cannot succeed,
to stab them, I fear I cannot hit."
Yàn Zǐ said:
"These are all men who forcefully attack strong enemies,
they observe no etiquette between elder and younger."
Therefore, he requested the Duke to send someone to subtly present them with two peaches,
and said:
"Why don't the three gentlemen assess their merit and eat the peaches?"
Gōngsūn Jiē looked up to the sky and sighed, saying:
"Yàn Zǐ is a wise man!
To have the Duke measure my merit,
not to accept the peach is to be without courage,
the warriors are many but the peaches are few,
why not assess the merit and eat the peach?
I once wrestled a boar and twice wrestled a young tiger,
with Jiē's merit, I can eat the peach and not share it with others."
He grasped the peach and stood up.
Tián Kāijiāng said:
"I have twice wielded weapons and repelled the three armies,
with Kāijiāng's merit,
I too can eat the peach,
and not share it with others."
He rose, clutching the peach. Gǔ Yě Zǐ said:
"I once followed you in crossing the river,
and a large turtle seized the left-side horse of your chariot and entered the current of Dǐzhù.
At that time,
I, though young, could not swim, but I dove
upstream a hundred paces, downstream nine *lǐ*,
caught the turtle and killed it, holding the horse's tail with my left hand,
and holding the turtle's head with my right, I leapt out like a crane.
All the people at the ford said:
'It's the River God!'
But as I saw it, it was only the head of a large turtle.
My merit is such that I can eat the peach and not share it with anyone.
Why don't you two return the peaches!"
He drew his sword and rose.
Gōngsūn Jiē and Tián Kāijiāng said:
"Our courage is not like yours, our merit does not match yours,
to take the peach without yielding is greed;
yet not to die, is lack of courage."
They both returned their peaches, slit their throats, and died.
Gǔ Yě Zǐ said:
"The two men died for this,
but I alone live; that is not benevolent;
to put others to shame with words,
and boast of one's own reputation is not righteous;
to resent what has been done,
and not to die, is lack of courage.
Although the two shared the peach and held fast to their principles,
I appropriated the peach all to myself and was fitting."
He also turned over his peach and hanged himself.
The messenger reported back:
"He is already dead."
The duke had him coffined in clothing and buried him with the rites of a gentleman.
2.25 *Jǐng Gōng登 Shè Sī Dé Yǒng Lì Shì Yǔ Zhī Tú Guó Yànzǐ Jiàn* (Duke Jing Ascends the Shooting Platform, Thinks of Obtaining Brave and Strong Warriors to Plan the State with, and Yànzǐ Advises Him)
Duke Jǐng ascended the shooting platform, and Yànzǐ arranged the rites and attended him.
The duke said:
"I am weary of the rites of selecting archers!
I wish to obtain brave warriors from all under Heaven and plan the state with them."
Yànzǐ replied:
"If a gentleman has no rites,
he is a commoner.
If a commoner has no rites, he is a bird or beast.
If ministers are too brave, they assassinate their ruler; if sons are too strong, they kill their elders.
However, they dare not do so because of rites.
Rites are what are used to govern the people,
reins are what are used to govern horses.
That one can govern a state without rites,
I, Ying, have never heard of such a thing."
Duke Jǐng said:
"Good."
Thereupon he decorated the shooting platform and changed the mats,
treating Yànzǐ as an honored guest and asking about rites all day long.
Inner Chapters, Asking about High (office)

3.1 *Zhuāng Gōng Wèn Wēi Dāngshì Fú Tiānxià Shí Yé Yànzǐ Duì Yǐ Xíng Yě* (Duke Zhuang Asks Whether Prestige That Influences the Age and Subdues All Under Heaven Is a Matter of Time; Yànzǐ Replies It Is a Matter of Conduct)
Zhuāng Gōng asked Yàn Zǐ, saying:
"To awe one's contemporaries and subdue the world,
is it a matter of timing?" Yàn Zǐ replied:
"It is a matter of conduct."
The Duke said:
"What conduct?"
He replied:
"One who can love the people within their own state,
can subdue the wickedness of those beyond its borders;
one who values the lives of their officers and people,
can restrain the perverse rebellion of violent states;
one who listens impartially and employs the worthy,
can awe the feudal lords;
one who is at peace with benevolence and righteousness and finds joy in benefiting the world,
can subdue the world.
One who cannot love the people within their own state,
cannot subdue the wickedness of those beyond its borders;
one who disregards the lives of their officers and people,
cannot restrain the perverse rebellion of violent states;
one who stubbornly rejects advice and is arrogant towards the worthy, cannot awe the feudal lords;
one who betrays benevolence and righteousness and covets fame and material gain,
cannot awe their contemporaries.
As for subduing the world,
this is the way to do it."
But the Duke did not heed this advice.
Yàn Zǐ retired and lived in seclusion.
The Duke appointed men of valor and strength,
And he lightly regarded the death of servants,
used soldiers without rest,
the state was exhausted and the people harmed.
Within a year, the common people were in great disorder,
and his own person, along with the Cuī Shì clan, met disaster.
A gentleman said:
"Exhausting loyalty without pre-arranged connections,
not accepting office without harboring desires for emolument,
Yàn Zǐ can be said to be incorruptible!"
3.2 《Zhuāng Gōng Wèn Fá Jìn Yàn Zǐ Duì Yǐ Bù Kě Ruò Bù Jì Guó Zhī Fú》
Duke Zhuāng was about to attack Jìn.
He asked Yàn Zǐ,
Yàn Zǐ replied,
"It is not permissible.
If a ruler is successful but his desires increase,
nurturing desire leads to arrogance.
One whose desires increase with success is in danger;
one who nurtures desire and becomes arrogant will be trapped.
Now, you are entrusting courageous and strong soldiers
to attack an enlightened ruler.
If it does not succeed, it is the state's fortune.
To have merit without virtue
worry will inevitably befall you."
The Duke changed his expression and was displeased.
Yàn Zǐ resigned from being a minister,
retreated, and lived in impoverished circumstances.
Lambsquarters and weeds grew beneath his hall,
brambles grew outside his gate.
Zhuāng Gōng 莊公 ultimately relied on brave and strong warriors.
He attacked Jìn 晉 to the west, seizing Zhāogē 朝歌.
He reached the Tài Háng 太行 and Mèng Mén 孟門 mountains.
He was victorious at Duì 兌, but within a year the people scattered.
He met his end at the hands of the Cuī 崔 clan.
Within a year of the Cuī 崔 clan's rise,
they drove out the various sons of the ruler [gōngzǐ 公子],
and the Qìng 慶 clan perished.
3.3 Jǐng Gōng 景公 Asks About Attacking Lǔ 魯, Yàn Zǐ 晏子 Responds That It Is Better to Cultivate Governance and Wait for Their Disorder
Jǐng Gōng 景公 raised an army, intending to attack Lǔ 魯.
He asked Yàn Zǐ 晏子 about it.
Yàn Zǐ 晏子 replied,
"It is not permissible.
The Duke of Lǔ 魯 is fond of righteousness, and the people support him.
Those who are fond of righteousness are secure.
Those who are supported are harmonious.
The governance of Bó Qín 伯禽 remains there.
Therefore, it cannot be attacked.
Attacking the righteous is inauspicious.
Endangering the secure will surely lead to distress.
Moreover, I have heard that
one who attacks others must have virtue sufficient to secure his own state
and governance sufficient to harmonize his own people.
When the state is secure and the people are harmonious,
then one can raise an army and punish the violent.
Now, you, my lord, are fond of wine and indulgence.
You have no virtue with which to secure the state.
Heavily taxing and extracting, using mandates and commands,
there is no way to harmonize the people.
If virtue cannot pacify them, there will be danger;
if government cannot harmonize them, there will be chaos.
Not avoiding the principles of danger and chaos,
yet wanting to attack peaceful and harmonious states,
is not permissible. It would be better to cultivate your government and wait for chaos in their ruler's reign.
When the people are separated from their ruler, and superiors resent their inferiors,
then attack them.
Then righteousness will be strong and benefits many,
with strong righteousness, enemies will be few,
and with many benefits, the people will rejoice."
The duke said:
"Good."
Consequently, he did not attack Lǔ.
3.4 《Duke Jǐng Conquers Lí, Asks About How To Reward, Yàn Zǐ Responds to Rewarding Officials Based on Strategy Victory》
Duke Jǐng attacked Lí and conquered it.
He asked Yàn Zǐ, saying:
"How should I reward Lí?"
He replied:
"I have heard that
those who conquer a state through strategy
should have their officials' stipends increased;
those who conquer a state through the people's strength
should have the people's benefits increased.
Thus, the superiors have abundant gains,
Below there is added profit,
The ruler enjoys the reputation thereof,
The ministers and subjects benefit from the substance thereof.
Therefore, those who use their wisdom do not steal labor,
Those who use their strength do not suffer hardship,
This is what the good conquerors of old did."
The Duke said:
"Good."
Thereupon, the ministers who conquered Lí,
And the soldiers of Dōngyì,
All received added profit.
This is the ruler alone possessing the reputation,
And profit flowing down to the people.
3.5 《Duke Jǐng Asked How the Sage Kings Acted, and Yàn Zǐ Replied by Satirizing the Decadent Age》
Duke Jǐng was outwardly arrogant towards the feudal lords,
And inwardly scornful of the common people,
He loved bravery and strength,
He esteemed music in order to indulge his desires,
The feudal lords were not pleased,
The common people were not close to him.
The Duke was troubled by this,
And asked Yàn Zǐ, saying:
"How did the sage kings of old
Act?"
Yàn Zǐ replied:
"Their conduct was just and without wickedness,
Therefore slanderers could not enter;
Not siding with cliques, not indulging in personal desires,
therefore, the troops of the crowd cannot find accommodation.
Being sparing with oneself and generous to the people,
therefore, those who hoard and collect cannot proceed.
Not encroaching upon the territory of large states,
not depleting the people of small states,
therefore, all the feudal lords desire his prestige.
Not coercing people with weapons and armor,
not intimidating people with numbers and strength,
therefore, all under Heaven desire his strength.
Virtuous conduct and moral teachings are extended to the feudal lords,
loving kindness and beneficial grace are extended to the common people,
therefore, all within the seas return to him like flowing water. Now, rulers of a declining age,
are perverse, wicked, and side with cliques,
therefore, the troops of slanderers and flatterers flourish.
They indulge themselves and nourish themselves, but regard the people with contempt,
therefore, those who hoard and collect proceed.
They encroach upon the territory of large states,
they deplete the people of small states,
therefore, the feudal lords do not desire their prestige.
They coerce people with weapons and armor,
they intimidate people with numbers and strength,
therefore, all under Heaven do not desire their strength.
Calamities are inflicted upon the feudal lords,
hardship and toil are imposed upon the common people,
therefore, enemies advance to attack,
all under Heaven will not come to the rescue,
noble relatives will be scattered and separated,
the people did not agree."
The Duke said:
"Then what should be done?"
Duó said:
"Please use humble words and generous gifts,
to persuade the feudal lords,
lighten punishments and reduce labor,
to apologize to the people,
would that be acceptable?" The Duke said:
"Yes."
Thereupon he used humble words and generous gifts,
and the feudal lords became attached to him,
he lightened punishments and reduced labor,
and the people became close to him,
therefore the small states came to court,
Yān and Lǔ together offered tribute.
Mòzǐ heard this and said:
"Yànzǐ understands the Dao,
the Dao lies in acting for others, and losing oneself.
Acting for others is weighty, acting for oneself is light.
Jǐng Gōng acted for himself,
and the small states did not agree,
(but when he) acted for others, the feudal lords served him,
thus the Dao lies in acting for others,
and the practice lies in reflecting on oneself.
Therefore Yànzǐ understands the Dao."
3.6 《Duke Jǐng asked about desiring to govern the state of Qí well in order to seek hegemony, and Yànzǐ replied that the offices were not complete》
Duke Jǐng asked Yànzǐ, saying:
"I wish to govern the state of Qi well,
and thus strive for hegemony among the feudal lords."
Yàn Zǐ replied:
"The offices are not complete.
I have reported this to you many times,
but you have not been willing to listen.
Therefore, I have heard that when Zhòng Ní's dwelling was lazy and careless,
and his integrity was not upright,
then Jì Cì and Yuán Xiàn attended him;
when his qi was stagnant and he felt ill, and his will was not clear,
then Zhòng Yóu and Bǔ Shāng attended him;
when his virtue was not abundant and his conduct was not generous,
then Yán Huí, Qiān, and Yōng attended him.
Now, Your Lordship has ten thousand courtiers,
and a thousand chariots,
yet the losses caused by bad governance to those below,
and the hardships falling upon the people are many,
yet there is no capable man who dares to report this.
Therefore, I say:
The offices are not complete." The Duke said:
"I wish to follow you, sir, and govern the state of Qi well. Is this possible?"
He replied:
"I have heard that a state must have complete offices
before its governance can be good."
The Duke's face changed and he was displeased,
saying:
"Although the state of Qi is small, can it be said that the offices are not complete?"
He replied:
"This is not something your servant can respond to.
In the past, my late lord, Duke Huán of Qí (齊桓公, Qí Huán Gōng), if his body was lazy and indolent,
and his eloquence was insufficient, then Xí Péng (隰朋) closely attended him.
If those around him made many mistakes, and judgments in legal cases were unjust,
then Xián Níng (弦甯) closely attended him. If the fields were not cultivated,
and the people were uneasy, then Níng Qī (甯戚) closely attended him.
If military officers were negligent, and soldiers were lazy,
then Wángzǐ Chéngfǔ (王子成甫) closely attended him.
If his living was dissolute and indolent, and those around him were fearful and apprehensive,
if there was excessive indulgence in music, and governance was neglected,
then Dōngguō Yá (東郭牙) closely attended him.
If his virtue and righteousness were lacking, and his trustworthiness and conduct declined,
then Guǎn Zǐ (管子) closely attended him.
My late lord was able to use the strengths of men to supplement their weaknesses,
and use the generosity of men to make up for their deficiencies.
Therefore, his eloquence reached far and wide without being rejected,
and his armies attacked the guilty without faltering.
Thus, the feudal lords paid homage to his virtue,
and the Son of Heaven bestowed sacrificial meat upon him.
Now, Your Lordship's faults and errors are many,
yet not a single scholar has informed you of them.
Therefore, it is said:
'The offices are not complete.'"
The Duke said,
"Well said."
3.7 *Jǐng Gōng Asks About Desiring to Use Guǎn Zhòng Like Huán Gōng to Achieve Hegemony; Yàn Zǐ Responds That It Is Not Possible*
Duke Jǐng (景公, Jǐng Gōng) asked Yàn Zǐ (晏子) , saying:
"In the past, my late lord, Duke Huán (桓公, Huán Gōng),
Having Guǎn Zhòng and Yí Wú to protect and govern the state of Qí,
they were able to accomplish military achievements and establish civil virtue,
uniting brothers, comforting and preserving Jì province,
Wú and Yuè received orders, Jīng and Chǔ were muddled with worry,
none failed to submit and be obedient,
diligently serving the Zhōu court, the Son of Heaven increased their merit.
Our late lord's manifest achievements were due to the power of Guǎn Zǐ.
Now I, the寡人, also desire to entrust the governance of the state of Qí to you, sir,
for you, sir, to assist me,
to make manifest the achievements of the late lord,
and to continue the work of Guǎn Zǐ."
Yàn Zǐ replied, saying:
"In the past, our late lord Huán Gōng was able to employ the worthy,
thus he had units of fifteen men, governing all the humble people,
the noble did not overbear the lowly, the rich did not become arrogant towards the poor,
merit was not overlooked due to fatigue, flattery did not spew out foolishness,
affairs were conducted without selfishness, judgments were heard without bias,
concubines within had no excessive food, ministers outside had no excessive salaries,
widowers and widows had no appearance of hunger;
not harming the people's wealth with indulgence in food and drink,
not exhausting the people's strength with extravagance in palaces and houses;
taking moderately from the people and distributing it widely,
the treasury had no hoarding, the granaries had no stored grain,
those above had no arrogant conduct, those below had no flattering virtue.
Because of this, Guǎn Zǐ was able to save the state of Qí from disaster,
and cause our late lord to be ranked with the Son of Heaven.
Now if you, lord, wish to make manifest the achievements of the late lord,
and continue the work of Guǎn Zǐ,
Then there would be no way to frequently avoid harming the common people,
no way to indulge in desires and playthings to cause resentment among the feudal lords.
Which minister would dare not embrace goodness and exert their utmost effort,
to comply with the ruler's intentions?
Now, you, my lord, alienate yourself from virtuous people and rely on slanderous flatterers;
you treat the people as if they cannot bear it, and your levies are as if they cannot be obtained;
you take heavily from the people and give sparingly to them,
you demand much from the feudal lords and slight them in your etiquette;
your storehouses are rotting away, and your etiquette is contrary to the feudal lords,
grain is stored deep, and resentment accumulates among the common people;
ruler and ministers are mutually hostile, and government and punishments are inconsistent:
I, your minister, fear that the state will be in danger of being lost,
and that you, my lord, will not be able to enjoy it.
Moreover, how can you possibly make manifest the glorious achievements of your late predecessor and continue the work of Guǎn Zǐ 管子!"
3.8 "Jǐng Gōng 景公 Asks 晏子 Yàn Zǐ Whether Jǔ 莒 or Lǔ 魯 Will Perish First; Yàn Zǐ Yàn Zǐ Replies That Lǔ 魯 Will Be Last, Jǔ 莒 First"
Jǐng Gōng 景公 asked Yàn Zǐ 晏子:
"Which will perish first, Jǔ 莒 or Lǔ 魯?"
He replied:
"According to my observation,
the common people of Jǔ 莒
change but do not transform, are greedy and fond of borrowing,
are haughty and brave but despise benevolence,
the officers are violent and quick to anger,
are easily angered and quickly exhausted.
Therefore, those above cannot nurture those below,
and those below cannot serve those above.
Those above and below cannot support each other,
then the essentials of governance are lost.
故以臣觀之也， Therefore, from your servant's perspective,
Jǔ qí xiān wáng." "Jǔ will be the first to perish."
Gōng yuē: The Duke said:
"Lǔ hé rú?" "What about Lǔ?"
Duì yuē: He replied:
"Lǔ zhī jūn chén, "The ruler and ministers of Lǔ,
yóu hào wèi yì, still have a fondness for practicing righteousness.
xià zhī tuǒ tuǒ yě, Those below are at ease,
yǎn rán guǎ wén, and they are generally ill-informed.
Shì yǐ shàng néng yǎng qí xià, Therefore, those above can nourish those below,
xià néng shì qí shàng, and those below can serve those above.
shàng xià xiāng shōu, Above and below support each other.
zhèng zhī dà tǐ cún yǐ. The general framework of governance is preserved.
Gù Lǔ yóu kě cháng shǒu, Therefore, Lǔ can still be defended for a long time,
rán qí yì yǒu yī yān. but it also has one flaw.
Bǐ Zōu Téng zhì bēn ér chū qí dì, Those of Zōu and Téng, like pheasants fleeing from their territory,
yóu chēng gōng hóu, still call themselves dukes and marquises.
xiǎo zhī shì dà, The small serve the large,
ruò zhī shì qiáng, jiǔ yǐ, the weak serve the strong, for a long time.
Bǐ Zhōu zhě, Yīn zhī shù guó yě, That Zhōu was a state established by the Yīn.
Lǔ jìn Qí ér qīn Yīn, Lǔ is close to Qí and aligned with the Yīn.
yǐ biàn xiǎo guó, To subdue small states,
ér bù fú yú lín, but not submitting to neighbors,
yǐ yuǎn wàng Lǔ, Looking at Lǔ from afar,
miè guó zhī dào yě. is the path to destroying the state.
Qí qí yǒu Lǔ yǔ Jǔ hū?" Will Qí possess Lǔ and Jǔ?"
Gōng yuē: The Duke said:
"Lǔ yǔ Jǔ zhī shì, "The affairs of Lǔ and Jǔ,
I, a man of little virtue, have heard of this.
My virtue is also meager.
Who will succeed in possessing the state of Qí in later generations?"
He replied:
"The descendants of Tián Wúyǔ will."
The Duke said:
"What is the reason for this?"
He replied:
"Your Highness's public generosity is small,
but your private generosity is great.
When bestowing favors upon the people,
in your dealings with gentlemen,
you use wealth without keeping it stored in baskets or chests.
The people of the state carry their children on their backs and lead them home to you,
like water flowing downwards.
To first give people benefits
and then decline their difficulties,
is that not rare?
If, indeed, you would not decline them
but instead care for them,
would it not be almost certain (that your descendants would continue to rule)!"
3.9 *Duke Jǐng asks what troubles governing the state, and Yànzǐ answers with "shrine rats and fierce dogs"*
Duke Jǐng asked Yànzǐ:
"What troubles governing a state?" Yànzǐ replied:
"The trouble is shrine rats."
The Duke said:
"What does that mean?"
Dùi yuē:
Now, the earth altar
is made by binding wood and coating it with mud.
Rats therefore go to lodge there.
If you smoke them out, you fear burning the wood.
If you flood it, you fear destroying the path.
This is why the rats cannot be killed,
because of the altar.
The state also has such things,
namely the ruler's close advisors.
In private, they conceal good and evil from the ruler.
In public, they sell power and influence to the common people.
If you do not punish them, they will cause chaos.
If you punish them, the ruler will use them as a defense.
The ruler relies on them.
These are also the altar rats of the state.
There was a man who sold wine.
His vessels were very clean and clear.
He placed a sign out that was very long.
But the wine turned sour and did not sell.
He asked the villagers the reason.
The villagers said,
'Your dog is fierce.
People carrying vessels try to enter,
intending to buy your wine,
but the dog greets them and bites them.
This is why the wine turns sour and does not sell.'
Now, the state also has fierce dogs,
Those in power are like this.
If there are scholars with Daoist arts
who wish to serve the ruler of a myriad chariots,
but those in power meet them and bite them,
they are also like fierce dogs of the state.
If those on the left and right are like shrine rats,
and those in power are like fierce dogs, (
how can the state be without trouble?)
Then scholars with Daoist arts will not be employed;
this is what the governance of the state should be concerned about."
3.10 *Jǐng Gōng* asked about ordering the *zhù shǐ* to seek blessings, and *Yàn Zǐ* disapproved, using constant terms to express guilt without seeking anything.
*Jǐng Gōng* asked *Yàn Zǐ*, saying,
"My spirit and vitality are declining, and I am very ill.
Now I want to prepare jade tokens, sacrificial animals,
and order the *zhù zōng* to present them to the Supreme God and ancestral temples.
Do you think rituals can be used to solicit blessings?"
*Yàn Zǐ* replied,
"I have heard that
when the former rulers sought blessings,
their policies certainly aligned with the people, and their actions certainly followed the spirits;
they regulated palaces and did not dare to engage in excessive cutting and felling
so as not to encroach upon the mountains and forests;
they regulated their diet and did not engage in excessive hunting and fishing
so as not to encroach upon the rivers and lakes;
the *zhù zōng* performed their duties,
expressing guilt and not daring to seek anything.
Therefore, the spirits and the people were both compliant,
but the mountains and rivers receive their stipends.
Now your governance, lord, goes against the people,
and your actions are contrary to the spirits;
grand palaces, much felling of trees,
in order to oppress the mountains and forests;
extravagant food and drink, much hunting and fishing,
in order to oppress the rivers and marshes.
Therefore, the people and the spirits both resent you,
and the mountains and rivers withhold their stipends,
the officials of transgression recommend punishment,
and the sacrificers pray for blessings,
(but) their intentions are reversed!"
The lord said:
"If not for you, master, I would have heard none of this,
I beg you to change my heart and alter my conduct."
Thereupon he abolished the hunts of Gōng Fù,
stopped the presentation of seafood,
the felling of trees was done in season,
the hunting and fishing were limited,
dwelling and eating,
were frugal without extravagance,
the sacrificers performed their duties,
confessing sins and daring not to ask for anything.
Therefore, neighboring states were wary of him,
the people were close to him,
and it declined after Yànzǐ's death.
3.11 《Duke Jǐng Asks How the Actions of Excellent Rulers of Antiquity Were, Yànzǐ Answers with Asking About Those Who Inquire About the Dao and Rectify Them》
Jǐng Gōng asked Yàn Zǐ,
"What were the actions of the great rulers of old?"
Yàn Zǐ replied,
"They were frugal with themselves but generous to the people,
restrained in their own lives but expansive in their influence on the world.
When they were in positions of authority,
they were able to clarify governance and implement teachings,
not relying on power to intimidate the world.
When they took wealth,
they considered what was available and what was not, equalized the poor and the rich,
not using it to indulge their desires.
Punishments did not spare the noble,
rewards did not overlook the humble.
They were not excessive in their pleasures,
nor did they escape into sorrow.
They exhausted their wisdom to guide the people,
yet did not boast about it;
they labored to serve the people,
yet did not demand anything in return.
Governance valued mutual benefit,
therefore those below did not consider harming each other as proper conduct.
Teachings valued mutual love,
therefore the people did not regard hating each other as reputable.
Penalties and punishments were in accordance with the law,
and the abolition of crimes was in accordance with the wishes of the people.
Therefore, the worthy held positions of authority without being ostentatious,
and the unworthy held positions below without resentment.
Within the four seas, within the altars of soil and grain,
the people who eat grain
are of one mind and share the same desires.
As for the governance of private families,
to provide substantial benefits during life and bequeath teachings after death,
this is the conduct of an enlightened ruler...
Your servant has heard that those who inquire about the Way correct themselves,
and those who listen to the Way become more tolerant.
Now, your taxes and levies are heavy, therefore the hearts of the people are estranged;
market transactions are disordered, therefore merchants cease to travel;
precious items fill your stores, therefore the wealth of families is exhausted.
Evil accumulates above, resentment is stored up among the people,
desires are fully satisfied among those at your side, slander and accusations fill the country,
and you, my lord, do not plan for this."
The lord said:
"Good."
Thereupon he ordered that precious items not be used,
he did not participate in public markets, he did not decorate the palace,
land projects were left unfinished, corvée labor was stopped, and taxes were lightened.
Those above and below practiced these measures, and the common people became close to one another.
3.12 *Jǐng Gōng* Asked *Yàn Zǐ* What Strategy Guaranteed Success in Planning and Execution, and *Yàn Zǐ* Responded with Deliberation Based on Righteousness and Reliance on the People.
*Jǐng Gōng* asked *Yàn Zǐ*:
"To have plans that are certain to succeed,
and affairs that are certain to be accomplished, is there a strategy for this?"
*Yàn Zǐ* replied,
"There is."
The lord said:
"Qí shù rúhé?" What is its technique?
Yàn Zǐ yuē: Yàn Zǐ said:
"Móudù yú yì zhě bì dé, "Those who plan and measure according to righteousness will surely succeed,
shì yīn yú mín zhě bì chéng." and those who base their actions on the people will surely accomplish [their goals]."
Gōng yuē: The Duke said:
"Xī wèi yě?" "What does that mean?"
Duì yuē: [Yàn Zǐ] replied:
"Qí móu yě, "When planning,
zuǒyòu wú suǒ xì, shàngxià wú suǒ mǐ, there is no attachment to those on the left or right, no bending to those above or below.
Qí shēng bù bèi, qí shí bù nì, Its pronouncements do not contradict [reason], and its substance does not go against [the people's will].
Móu yú shàng, bù wéi tiān, When planning with superiors, it does not violate Heaven;
móu yú xià, bù wéi mín, when planning with inferiors, it does not violate the people.
Yǐ cǐ mó zhě bì dé yǐ; Those who plan in this way will surely succeed.
shì dà zé lì hòu, If the undertaking is large, the benefits will be great;
shì xiǎo zé lì báo, if the undertaking is small, the benefits will be meager.
Chēng shì zhī dàxiǎo, Weighing the size of the undertaking,
quán lì zhī qīngzhòng, and assessing the weight of the benefits,
guó yǒu yì láo, the state will have justified labor,
mín yǒu jiā lì, and the people will have increased benefits.
Yǐ cǐ jǔshì zhě bì chéng yǐ. Those who undertake affairs in this way will surely succeed.
Fú táoyì ér mó, suī chéng bù ān; Indeed, if one plans while abandoning righteousness, even if successful, one will not be secure;
àomín jǔshì, suī chéng bù róng. if one undertakes affairs while being arrogant towards the people, even if successful, one will not be honored.
Gù chén wén yì, Therefore, I have heard that righteousness
mó zhī fǎ yě, mín, shì zhī běn yě, is the principle of planning, and the people are the foundation of affairs.
Gù fǎnyì ér mó, bèi mín ér dòng, Therefore, if one plans against righteousness and acts against the people,
wèi wén cún zhě yě. I have never heard of such a [state] surviving.
Xī sāndài zhī xīng yě, In the past, when the Three Dynasties flourished,
mó bì dù yú yì, shì bì yīn yú mín. their plans always measured up to righteousness, and their actions always relied on the people.
And when it declines, those who offer plans betray righteousness,
and those who initiate projects harm the people.
Therefore, measuring righteousness and considering the people
are the arts of planning affairs."
The Duke said:
"I am not wise;
I hear good advice but do not act on it.
What is the danger?"
He replied:
"The best ruler is completely good; the next best sometimes succeeds and sometimes fails;
the next best is stubborn in evil and ashamed to ask questions.
The completely good ruler can control [the situation];
the sometimes-succeeding,
sometimes-asking ruler,
although in daily danger,
can still preserve himself until death;
the ashamed-to-ask ruler
cannot protect himself.
Now, although you are in danger,
you can still preserve yourself until death."
3.13 *Jǐng Gōng* asks what constitutes a good ruler of a state, and *Yàn Zǐ* replies with recommending virtuous officials and capable administrators.
*Jǐng Gōng* asked *Yàn Zǐ* saying:
"In governing the state and managing the people,
what is a good way to be a ruler of a state?"
*Yàn Zǐ* replied:
"Raise up the virtuous to oversee the state,
and appoint the capable to manage the people, and that is the proper way.
"If you promote the worthy and employ the capable, the people will be with you."
The Duke said,
"Even if there are worthy and capable people, how would I know them?"
Yàn Zǐ replied,
"If they are worthy but remain hidden, what use is their worth?
My lord also does not concern himself with this,
therefore you do not know."
The Duke said,
"I ask how to seek out the worthy."
He replied,
"Observe them through their associations,
speak of them through their actions.
Your Lord should not use flowery rhetoric to determine their conduct,
and do not let praise or slander define their character.
In this way, they will not act to promote their reputation,
nor conceal their desires to please the ruler.
Therefore, when influential, observe what they recommend;
when impoverished, observe what they do not do;
when wealthy, observe what they share; when poor, observe what they do not take.
The highest scholar is difficult to advance and easy to retire;
the next is easy to advance and easy to retire;
the lowest is easy to advance and difficult to retire.
If you choose men based on these several criteria, would that not be acceptable?"
3.14 Duke Jǐng asked Yàn Zǐ whether it was difficult for a ruler and minister to be respected and honored, and Yàn Zǐ replied that it was easy.
Duke Jǐng asked Yàn Zǐ,
"For a ruler to be respected and the people secure,
for a minister to govern well and be honored,
is it difficult or easy?"
Yàn Zǐ 晏子 replied,
"Easy."
The Duke said,
"How so?"
He replied,
"If the ruler economizes on his own extravagance to care for the people,
then his person will be honored and the people will be at peace.
If the minister is loyal and trustworthy and does not overstep his duties,
then affairs will be well-governed and his person will be honored."
The Duke then asked,
"What actions by a ruler lead to danger?
What actions by a minister lead to ruin?"
Yàn Zǐ 晏子 replied,
"For a ruler,
to heavily tax and extort while claiming it is for the people,
to promote slanderers and flatterers while claiming he is employing the virtuous,
to distance himself from the just and upright while claiming it is because they are disobedient—
if a ruler acts in these three ways, he will be in danger.
For a minister,
to form cliques to seek advancement,
to overstep his duties,
to prevent subordinates from concealing profits and seek more for himself,
to follow the ruler
without pointing out his mistakes in order to seek favor—
if a minister acts in these three ways, he will be ruined. Therefore, an enlightened ruler does not view the people with a biased eye,
adheres to principles without wavering,
establishes laws and standards without violating them,
and if he seeks something from the people,
不以身害之， Do not harm them with your own person;
是故刑政安於下， therefore, punishments and governance are peaceful below,
民心固於上。 and the people's hearts are secure above.
故察士不比周而進， Therefore, discerning officers do not advance by currying favor,
不為苟而求， nor do they seek [advancement] through insincerity.
言無陰陽，行無內外， Their words are without hidden meanings, their actions are without internal or external [duplicity].
順則進，否則退， If [their advice is] followed, they advance; if not, they retreat.
不與上行邪， They do not engage in wickedness with their superiors.
是以進不失廉， Therefore, in advancing, they do not lose their integrity,
退不失行也。」 and in retreating, they do not lose their virtuous conduct."
3.15 《Jǐng Gōng Wèn Tiānxià zhī Suǒyǐ Cúnwáng Yàn Zǐ Duì Yǐ Liù Shuō》 3.15 《Duke Jǐng asked about the reasons for the survival and demise of states; Yàn Zǐ replied with six explanations》
景公問晏子曰： Jǐng Gōng asked Yàn Zǐ, saying:
「寡人持不仁，其無義耳也。 "I hold to unbenevolence; surely I am without righteousness.
不然，北面與夫子而義。」 If not, then to face north towards you, Master, is righteous."
晏子對曰： Yàn Zǐ replied, saying:
「嬰、人臣也， "Yīng is a minister.
公曷為出若言？」 Why does Your Lordship utter such words?"
公曰： The Duke said:
「請終問天下之所以存亡。」 "Please, I will finish asking about the reasons for the survival and demise of states."
晏子曰： Yàn Zǐ said:
「縵密不能， Those incapable of fine weaving,
蔍苴不學者詘，身無以用人， those who do not learn coarse matting are demeaned; those who personally have no way to employ people
而又不為人用者卑。 and are also not employed by others are lowly.
善人不能戚，惡人不能踈者危。 Those who cannot be intimate with good people, and cannot be distant from bad people are in danger.
交游朋友，從無以說於人， Those who, in associating with friends, never have anything to persuade others with,
又不能說人者窮。 and also cannot persuade people, are impoverished.
事君要利， In serving their lord, seeking benefit,
大者不得，小者不為者餧。 those who do not obtain great things and do not do small things are hungry.
Cultivating the Way and establishing righteousness,
those who are too great to be controlled or too small to be attached to will perish.
This is enough to observe survival and destruction."
3.16 《Jǐng Gōng Asks About the Constant Conduct of a Gentleman, Yàn Zǐ Replies with Three Things》
Jǐng Gōng asked Yàn Zǐ, saying:
"What is the constant conduct of a gentleman like?" Yàn Zǐ replied:
"If one's attire is improper, he would not dare to enter the court;
if his words are unrighteous, he would not dare to demand from the ruler;
if his personal conduct is not compliant and his handling of affairs is unjust,
he would not dare to preside over the people.
If one's attire is always proper, then the court will have no strange or eccentric clothing;
if his words are always righteous, then the subordinates will have no false reports to their superiors;
if his personal conduct is compliant and his handling of affairs is just,
then the state will have no party affiliations.
These three things
are the constant conduct of a gentleman."
3.17 《Jǐng Gōng Asks How a Wise Ruler Governs the State, Yàn Zǐ Replies with Appointing the Worthy and Loving the People》
Jǐng Gōng asked Yàn Zǐ, saying:
"How does a wise ruler govern the state?"
Yàn Zǐ replied:
"His government employs the worthy, his conduct loves the people,
his taxation of the people is moderate, and his self-cultivation is frugal;
when in a position of power, he does not offend those below him, and when governing, he is not arrogant towards the poor;
those who follow wickedness and harm the people are guilty,
and those who promote good and point out faults are rewarded.
His government is harsh on those above and generous to those below,
forgiving offenses and helping the poor;
Do not increase rewards because of joy, and do not increase punishments because of anger;
do not indulge desires to burden the people, and do not cultivate anger to endanger the state;
the ruler has no arrogant behavior, and the subordinates have no flattering virtue;
the ruler has no private righteousness, and the subordinates do not steal power;
the ruler has no decaying storehouses, and the subordinates have no people suffering from cold and hunger;
do not engage in arrogant behavior but value administration;
the people will be peaceful and happy and hold their superiors in esteem.
Such is the way a wise ruler governs a state."
3.18 *Jǐng Gōng* asks what the wise king taught the people, *Yàn Zǐ* replies by first acting righteously.
*Jǐng Gōng* asked *Yàn Zǐ*, saying:
"What did the wise king teach the people?" *Yàn Zǐ* replied, saying:
"Clarify the decrees and instructions, and precede them with righteous actions;
nourish the people without being harsh, and prevent wrongdoing with laws and punishments;
what is demanded from those below must first be practiced by those above;
what is forbidden to the people must not be done by the ruler himself.
Protect the people's wealth and do not diminish it for personal gain,
establish standards and laws and do not violate them with wickedness,
if something is demanded from the people but the ruler does not harm them,
then those below will be encouraged to follow his teachings.
Assign tasks according to ability,
listen to appropriate advice to prevent evil,
do not exhaust the people with labor,
do not harm them with punishments,
if something is forbidden to the people,
do not act against them in any affair,
then those below will not dare to offend their superiors.
In ancient times, customs differed every hundred *lǐ*,
A thousand *lǐ* and different customs arise; therefore, enlightened rulers cultivate the Way,
unifying the people with common customs.
Those above use love for the people as the law, those below use mutual affection as righteousness.
Therefore, the world does not abandon each other.
This is how enlightened rulers teach the people."
3.19 "Duke Jing asked what a loyal minister should do when serving his lord, and Yanzi replied that he should not let his lord fall into difficulty."
Duke Jǐng asked Yànzǐ, saying:
"What should a loyal minister do when serving his lord?" Yànzǐ replied abruptly:
"When there is trouble, he does not die;
when his lord flees, he does not see him off."
The Duke was displeased
and said:
"The ruler divides land and enfeoffs him,
bestows titles and ennobles him.
When the ruler is in trouble, he does not die;
when his lord flees, he does not see him off.
What is the explanation for this?"
He replied:
"If his words are heeded,
he will have no trouble throughout his life;
why should the minister die?
If his plans are followed,
he will not have to flee throughout his life;
why should the minister see him off?
If his words are not heeded,
to die when there is trouble is to die in vain.
shì wàng sǐ yě;
If one's counsel is not heeded,
yet one escorts the ruler in flight,
this is deceit and falsehood.
Therefore, a loyal minister
is one who can offer good advice to the ruler,
but cannot allow himself to be trapped in difficulty with the ruler."
3.20 *Jǐng Gōng* Asks What the Actions of a Loyal Minister Should Be, *Yàn Zǐ* Responds That He Does Not Act Wrongly With the Ruler
*Jǐng Gōng* asked *Yàn Zǐ*, saying:
"What should be the actions of a loyal minister?"
He replied:
"Not concealing the ruler's faults,
advising him to his face,
not being ostentatious outwardly;
selecting the worthy and advancing the able,
not being partial inwardly;
matching one's abilities to one's position,
calculating one's abilities to receive remuneration;
seeing the worthy and not occupying a position above them,
receiving remuneration not exceeding one's due;
not using the ruler's authority for one's own actions,
not using one's position to feign loyalty;
not suppressing the worthy to obscure one's own strengths,
not oppressing subordinates to flatter superiors;
when the ruler is present, not serving the heir apparent,
when the state is in danger, not making alliances with the feudal lords;
if things go smoothly, then advance; if not, then retreat;
not acting wrongly with the ruler."
3.21 *Jǐng Gōng* Asks How a Sycophant Serves the Ruler, *Yàn Zǐ* Responds That He Is Trusted by a Foolish Ruler
Jǐng Gōng asked: "How do flatterers serve their ruler?"
Yàn Zǐ replied:
"Their intentions are difficult [to discern], but the difficulty doesn't end there.
They clearly state their actions to adorn themselves,
they feign desires to please others,
they make their associations strict to show their love;
they observe what the ruler desires,
and subtly provide opportunities for it,
they seek to make the ruler press them,
and secretly assist him in it;
inwardly they value rank and emolument,
but outwardly they belittle them to feign virtue,
they serve those around the ruler,
but outwardly show honesty to the prince to feign incorruptibility;
they seek the ruler's approval and attention,
and use favor to seek advancement;
they act proudly of their emolument to seek more,
they decline responsibilities to seek importance;
they are skilled at taking,
and stingy at giving;
they rejoice in the new,
and neglect the old;
they are miserly with wealth,
and meager in giving;
they look at the poor and destitute as if they don't know them,
and rush towards profit as if they can't catch up;
they use external relations to promote themselves,
and turn their backs on relatives to enrich themselves;
they accumulate abundant resources,
and proclaim the virtue of generosity and compassion;
they criticize praise based on emotion,
but their words do not match their actions,
they partake in timely discussions,
and to enjoy discussing the virtues and vices of others;
if they themselves possess something,
they find it easy to criticize others;
if they themselves lack something,
they find it easy to demand it of others;
their words are strong and believable,
their advancement is quick, humble and compliant:
these are the actions of a flatterer.
They are punished by enlightened rulers,
but trusted by foolish rulers."
3.22 "Duke Jing Asks What Befalls a Sage Who Does Not Attain His Ambitions, and Yànzǐ Replies that He Does Not Allow Himself to be Corrupted by the World"
Duke Jǐng asked Yànzǐ, saying: "What happens to a sage who does not attain his ambitions?"
Yànzǐ replied:
"When the ruler acts against the seasons,
governs against the spirits,
and exhausts the people with taxes;
when the four seasons are out of order,
and the deities are all resentful;
when those who speak faithfully are not listened to,
and those who recommend good men are not employed,
when those who flatter are rewarded,
To rescue those who are lost is a crime.
Therefore, the sage lies low, concealing himself in seclusion,
not interfering with his superiors,
purifying himself and adhering to the Dao,
not joining the world in its descent into wickedness.
Thus, though humble, he does not lose his righteousness;
though weary, he does not lose his integrity.
This is what it means for a sage to be unsuccessful."
Gōng (公) said, "What is it like for a sage to be successful?"
He replied,
"When the world is well-ordered and the government is peaceful,
undertakings are in harmony with Heaven,
taxation is harmonious with the people, the common people
are happy with their government,
and those far away cherish his virtue;
the four seasons do not lose their order,
wind and rain do not descend with cruelty;
Heaven reveals signs and bestows blessings,
Earth nourishes and provides all things;
the spirits bestow blessings without extravagance,
and the people submit to instruction without deceit;
in governance, there are no grounds for complaint,
and in the land, there are no idle people:
this is what it means for a sage to be successful."
3.23 "Jǐng Gōng (景公) Asks About How Ancient Rulers and People Managed States Without Danger or Weakness – Yàn Zǐ’s (晏子) Reply About Wén Wáng (文王)"
Jǐng Gōng (景公) asked Yàn Zǐ (晏子), "In ancient times, how did rulers and people become endangered,
and how did states become weakened?
"How can one lose it?"
Yàn Zǐ replied,
"I have heard that,
those who govern a state with evil,
and harmonize the people with violence, are in danger.
Those who cultivate the Way to seek profit,
and who turn to evil after gaining their desires, are weak.
In ancient times, King Wén cultivated virtue,
not to seek profit.
He destroyed violence, not by complying with Zhòu,
he offended the violence of Marquis Chóng,
and reverenced the minced meat of Méi Bó.
Therefore, the lords were clear about his actions,
and the people understood his virtue.
Thus, he ruled the people without danger,
and used the state without weakening it."
3.24 《Duke Jǐng Asks Yàn Zǐ How Those Who Governed States in Ancient Times Employed People; Yàn Zǐ Replies That People Have Different Abilities》
Duke Jǐng asked Yàn Zǐ,
"How did those who governed states and ruled the people in ancient times
employ people?"
Yàn Zǐ replied,
"Land is not uniformly suitable,
yet if you assign one single task to it,
it is impossible to expect that all will flourish.
People have different abilities,
yet if you assign one single task to them,
it is impossible to expect them to accomplish it perfectly.
To demand without end,
Even the wise have things they cannot give;
seeking from them will never be satisfied;
even heaven and earth cannot provide for everything.
Therefore, the enlightened king's employment of people
does not keep flatterers close at hand,
nor does he govern his court with those who form factions;
he employs people for their strengths
and does not force their weaknesses;
he employs people for their skills
and does not force their clumsiness.
This is the general principle of employing people."
3.25 《Duke Jing Asks How the Ancients Scattered Their People, and Yanzi Responds That Now They Hear the Duke's Orders as if from an Enemy》
Duke Jǐng asked Yàn Zǐ, saying:
"Those in ancient times who scattered their people and lost their states,
what were their usual practices?"
Yàn Zǐ replied:
"The state is poor but loves grandeur,
wisdom is shallow but loves to be autocratic;
the noble and the lowly have no affection for each other,
the great ministers have no courtesy;
valuing flattery and despising the worthy,
delighting in rudeness and trifling with the common people;
the state has no constant laws,
the people have no economic structure;
loving debate as wisdom, oppressing the people as loyalty,
indulging in drink and forgetting the state,
loving war and forgetting the people;
To be swift in punishing crimes,
yet slow in bestowing rewards;
to rejoice in others' sorrow,
to profit from others' difficulties;
if virtue is insufficient to win people's hearts,
if governance is insufficient to benefit the people;
if rewards are insufficient to encourage good,
if punishments are insufficient to prevent wrong:
these are the actions that lead to the downfall of a state.
Now the people hear the duke's commands as if they were the enemy and a grudge,
this is the usual behavior of those in ancient times who alienated their people,
and caused their states to crumble and be lost."
3.26 Duke Jǐng asks about wanting to harmonize his ministers and be close to his inferiors, Yànzi responds with trustworthiness, obedience, frugality and moderation.
Duke Jǐng asked Yànzi, saying:
"I want to harmonize my ministers and be close to my inferiors, what should I do?"
Yànzi replied, saying:
"If the ruler obtains ministers and employs them,
speaks truthfully with them,
certainly obeys their commands,
forgives their faults,
entrusts them with great responsibilities without excessive blame, ensures that close retainers do not seek favor,
does not impoverish their families with excessive desires, does not trust slanderers to harm their hearts,
so that their families are self-sufficient without seeking external gains,
and serving the ruler does not depend on personal connections for advancement,
then the ministers will be harmonious. Be frugal in levies and taxes,
moderate in the use of wealth and resources,
construction work should not be protracted,
"Cause the people not to exhaust their strength,
regulate the hundred officials appropriately,
reduce tariffs at the passes and markets,
and do not monopolize the profits from the mountains, forests, banks, and marshes.
bù zhuān qí lì,
Lead and govern the people,
do not cause them trouble and disorder,
know their poverty and wealth,
and do not cause them to suffer from cold and hunger,
then the people will be close (to you)."
The Duke said:
"Good!
I have heard your command."
Therefore, he ordered the princes not to have external personal visits,
and kept Liángqiū Jù at a distance, not allowing him to receive repayment.
He regulated the hundred officials appropriately,
reduced tariffs at the passes and markets,
did not restrict the banks and marshes,
redressed those who were wrongly accused,
and let those detained in prison make requests.
3.27 "Duke Jǐng asked about the way to obtain the virtuous, and Yànzǐ replied by recommending them through words and examining them through deeds."
Duke Jǐng asked Yànzǐ, saying:
"What is the way to obtain the virtuous?"
Yànzǐ replied, saying:
"Recommend them through words,
examine them through deeds,
if they can understand,
Then, valuing them and drawing near to them,
being close to them without disgracing them, in order to acquire people,
then one obtains the way to [acquire] the worthy.
Therefore, an enlightened ruler, residing above,
reduces his officials but increases his actions,
is unskilled in writing but skilled in affairs,
if speech does not hit the mark, he does not speak,
if action does not accord with the law, he does not act."
3.28 *Jǐng Gōng* asks what a subject uses to repay his ruler, and *Yàn Zǐ* replies with repaying with virtue.
*Jǐng Gōng* asked *Yàn Zǐ*, saying:
"How does a subject repay his ruler?" *Yàn Zǐ* replied, saying:
"Although your subject does not know,
he must strive to repay his ruler with virtue.
When a scholar meets a ruler with the *dào*,
then he complies with his commands;
when he meets a ruler without the *dào*,
then he contends against his unrighteousness.
Therefore, the ruler chooses his subjects and employs them,
and although the subject is lowly,
he also gets to choose his ruler and serve him."
3.29 *Jǐng Gōng* asks what the worries are in governing a state and overseeing the people, and *Yàn Zǐ* replies with three worries.
*Jǐng Gōng* asked *Yàn Zǐ*, saying:
"In governing a state and overseeing the people,
what are the worries?" *Yàn Zǐ* replied, saying:
"The worries are three:
loyal subjects are not trusted,
One concern;
trustworthy ministers being disloyal,
a second concern;
ruler and ministers having different intentions,
a third concern.
Therefore, a wise ruler in a high position
has no loyal people who are not trustworthy,
and no trustworthy people who are not loyal.
Thus, ruler and ministers share the same desires,
and the common people have no grievances."
3.30 *Jǐng Gōng* asks what concerns there are in governance, *Yàn Zǐ* replies that good and evil are not distinguished.
*Jǐng Gōng* asked *Yàn Zǐ*, saying:
"What concerns are there in governing?"
*Yàn Zǐ* replied, saying:
"The concern is that good and evil are not distinguished."
*Gōng* said:
"How can one discern them?"
He replied, saying:
"Carefully select those on your left and right.
If those on your left and right are good,
then all the officials will each obtain what is appropriate for them,
and good and evil will be distinguished."
*Kǒng Zǐ* heard this and said:
"These words are indeed trustworthy!
If good advances,
then evil will have no way to enter;
if evil advances,
then good will have no way to enter."
Inner Chapters, Questioning from Below
4.1 《Duke Jing Asks How to Cultivate the Tours of Former Kings, and Yanzi Responds with Inspecting Farming and Harvests》
Duke Jǐng went on a tour and
asked Yàn Zǐ, saying:
"I wish to travel south along the coast,
reaching Lángyá.
How should I, the寡人 (guǎrén, a humble term for "I" used by rulers), cultivate [my tour]
to be like the tours of the former kings?"
Yàn Zǐ bowed twice and said:
"Excellent!
Your question is good.
I have heard that the Son of Heaven's visits to the feudal lords are called patrols (巡狩 xúnshòu),
and the feudal lords' visits to the Son of Heaven are called reporting duties (述職 shùzhí).
Therefore, inspecting farming in spring and supplementing what is insufficient is called游 (yóu, "tour").
Inspecting harvests in autumn and assisting those in need is called 豫 (yù, "preparation" or "provision").
The Summer Ode says:
'If our lord does not游 (yóu),
how shall we rest?
If our lord does not 豫 (yù),
how shall we be helped?
One 游 (yóu) and one 豫 (yù),
are the standards for the feudal lords.'
Now your tour is not like that.
The army marches and consumes much food,
the poor and suffering are not helped,
and the laborers are not given rest.
To linger in high places for a long time without returning is called 流 (liú, "drifting").
To linger in time and not return is called indulgence;
to follow hunting and not return is called dissipation;
to follow pleasure and not return is called ruin.
In ancient times, sage kings had no wandering indulgences,
nor dissipated and ruinous behavior."
The Duke said,
"Good."
He ordered officials to calculate the Duke's allotted grain,
and to register the number of the elderly and young, and the poor people.
The official then personally oversaw the distribution of grain from the granary,
giving three thousand *zhōng* to the poor.
The Duke himself saw seventy disabled and elderly people,
assisted and provided for them, and then returned.
4.2 *Jǐng Gōng* Asks What Made *Huán Gōng* a Hegemon, *Yàn Zǐ* Answers by Lowering Himself to the Worthy
*Jǐng Gōng* asked *Yàn Zǐ*, saying:
"In the past, my late lord *Huán Gōng*,
was fond of drinking wine to the fullest extent of pleasure,
ate delicacies spread over a square *zhàng*,
and was indiscriminate in his love of women,
like this.
How could he lead the feudal lords to pay homage to the Son of Heaven?"
*Yàn Zǐ* replied,
"In the past, my late lord *Huán Gōng*,
changed customs with governance,
and lowered himself to the worthy.
*Guǎn Zhòng*,
was a traitor to the ruler.
Knowing that his abilities were sufficient to secure the country and accomplish great deeds,
he therefore welcomed him in the suburbs of Lǔ,
personally drove the chariot for him,
and treated him with respect in the temple.
Another day, the ruler passed by Kāngzhuāng,
heard Nìng Qī singing,
stopped the chariot to listen to him,
and recognized in him the demeanor of a virtuous man.
He promoted him to the position of Dàtián.
Because the former ruler, upon seeing a virtuous man, did not detain him,
and employed capable men without negligence,
the people cherished him in internal affairs,
and the feudal lords feared him in military expeditions.
Now, Your Lordship has heard of the mistakes of the former ruler,
but is unable to understand his great virtue.
Duke Huán's hegemony,
what doubts do you have about it?"
4.3 *Jǐng Gōng Asks About Wanting to Catch Up to Duke Huán's Descendants, Yàn Zǐ Replies That He Employs the Wrong People*
Duke Jǐng asked Yàn Zǐ, saying:
"In the past, my late ruler, Duke Huán,
with three hundred chariots,
nine times united the feudal lords and rectified the world.
Now, I have a thousand chariots,
can I catch up to the descendants of my late ruler, Duke Huán?"
Yàn Zǐ replied, saying:
"Duke Huán, with three hundred chariots,
nine times united the feudal lords and rectified the world,
had Bào Shū on his left and Zhòng Fù on his right.
"Now, Your Lordship has actors on your left and jesters on your right,
slanderers in front and flatterers behind.
How then can you attain the legacy of Duke Huán?"
4.4 *Jǐng Gōng* Asks About Upright Governance and Lasting Rule, *Yàn Zǐ* Responds with the Analogy of Water
*Jǐng Gōng* asked *Yàn Zǐ*, saying:
"Upright governance and lasting rule,
what is its principle of operation?"
*Yàn Zǐ* replied, saying:
"Its principle of operation is water.
How beautiful is water, so clear!
Its turbidity is not allowed to remain.
Its clarity leaves nothing uncleansed.
Therefore it lasts long."
The Duke said:
"Upright governance that quickly perishes, what is its principle of operation?"
He replied, saying:
"Its principle of operation is stone.
How solid is stone, so unyielding!
Looking at it, it is hard; feeling it, it is hard.
Inside and out, it is all hard, and cannot last long.
Therefore it quickly perishes."
4.5 *Jǐng Gōng* Asks About the Way to Be a Minister, *Yàn Zǐ* Responds with Nine Principles
*Jǐng Gōng* asked *Yàn Zǐ*, saying:
"I would like to ask about the way to be a minister."
*Yàn Zǐ* replied, saying:
"Upon seeing good, one must communicate it,
not be selfish with its benefits,
recommend the good without taking credit for it;
To be in a position commensurate with one's ability
and not strive for advancement through improper means;
to bestow emoluments according to the task at hand
and not acquire gains through improper means;
to value the honorable and demote the base,
without going against their natural order;
to place the virtuous and the unworthy
without disrupting their proper sequence;
fertile and profitable lands
are not made into personal fiefs;
men of virtuous qualities
are not made into personal retainers;
the ruler uses their words,
and the people receive their benefits,
yet one does not boast of one's accomplishments.
This is the way of a minister."
4.6 *Jǐng Gōng* Asks Whether the Worthy and Unworthy Can Be Learned, *Yàn Zǐ* Replies with Exertion Being Paramount
*Jǐng Gōng* asked *Yàn Zǐ*, saying:
"Human nature has the worthy and unworthy; can these be learned?"
*Yàn Zǐ* replied, saying:
"The *Shī* (Book of Odes) says:
'High mountains, one looks up to them;
great roads, one travels them.'
The worthy, that is their kind of person.
Therefore, among the feudal lords who stand together,
the one who is virtuous and does not become lazy becomes the leader;
among the scholars who study together,
the one who perseveres in virtue to the end becomes the teacher."
4.7 *Jǐng Gōng* Asks About Enriching the People and Pacifying the Masses, *Yàn Zǐ* Responds with Tempering Desires and Listening Impartially
*Jǐng Gōng* asked *Yàn Zǐ*, saying:
"Is enriching the people and pacifying the masses difficult?"
*Yàn Zǐ* replied, saying:
"It is easy. If you temper desires, then the people will be rich;
if you listen impartially, then the people will be at peace.
Simply practice these two things."
4.8 *Jǐng Gōng* Asks What Kind of State Can Be Called Peaceful, *Yàn Zǐ* Responds with Internal Peace in Governance and External Adherence to Righteousness
*Jǐng Gōng* asked *Yàn Zǐ*, saying:
"What kind of state can be called peaceful?"
*Yàn Zǐ* replied, saying:
"Those below do not avoid speaking frankly;
officials do not resent governance;
learned men are not ostentatious;
poor people do not complain;
joy and pleasure do not lead to excessive rewards;
anger and resentment do not lead to excessive punishments;
those above are courteous to scholars;
those below are kind to the people;
a large territory does not encroach on smaller ones;
a strong military does not threaten the weak;
the common people find peace in their government internally,
and externally adhere to righteousness:
This can be called peaceful."
4.9 *Jǐng Gōng* Asks Which of the Lords is in Danger, *Yàn Zǐ* Responds that *Jǔ* Will Perish First
*Jǐng Gōng* asked *Yàn Zǐ*, saying:
"In this present time,
which of the lords is in danger?"
Yàn Zǐ answered,
"Jǔ is about to perish!"
The Duke said,
"Why?"
He replied,
"Its land is encroached upon by Qí,
its resources are exhausted by Jìn,
therefore it will perish."
4.10 *Yàn Zǐ's Mission to Wú, the King of Wú Asks About When to Stay and When to Leave, Yàn Zǐ Responds by Observing the Order or Disorder of the State*
Yàn Zǐ was on a diplomatic mission to Wú. The King of Wú said,
"Sir, a *dàfū*, by your lord's command you honor my humble territory,
bestowing gifts upon me. I have received them.
I wish to ask you a private question."
Yàn Zǐ stepped back deferentially and replied,
"Yīng is a lowly servant from the North,
privileged to carry out my lord's command, hastening to your court.
I fear that my words may not be precise, and I might be ridiculed by the lower officials.
I worry that I might not know how to answer."
The King of Wú said,
"I have heard of you for a long time, sir.
Now I have the opportunity to meet you.
I wish to complete my question."
Yàn Zǐ moved aside from his mat and replied,
"I respectfully accept your command."
The King of Wú said,
"Under what circumstances is a state worth staying in,
and under what circumstances is it worth leaving?"
Yàn Zǐ answered,
"Yīng has heard that if relatives and distant relations are properly placed in their order,
great ministers are able to fully express their loyalty,
the people have no grievances against the government, and the state has no cruel punishments,
then one can remain.
Therefore, a virtuous person cherishes a ruler who does not act against reason,
and occupies a position in a well-governed state.
If relatives and distant relations are not properly placed in their order,
great ministers are unable to fully express their loyalty,
the people have many grievances against the government,
and the state has cruel punishments,
then one should leave.
Therefore, a virtuous person does not cherish the emoluments of a tyrannical ruler,
nor does he occupy a position in a chaotic state."
4.11 *Wú* King Asks for the Way to Preserve Power and Strength Without Losing It; *Yàn Zǐ* Answers by Prioritizing the People over Oneself
Yàn Zǐ was on a diplomatic mission to *Wú*.
The King of *Wú* said,
"May I ask what is the way to preserve power and strength for a long time without losing it?"
Yàn Zǐ answered,
"Prioritize the people over oneself,
prioritize bestowing benefits over punishments;
the strong do not bully the weak,
the noble do not look down on the humble,
the rich do not despise the poor;
the common people advance together,
the officials do not encroach,
the people are harmonious and the government is peaceful;
do not use power and strength to repel the ruler of another,
He does not use his strength to seize the lands of others;
his use of law is to stop violence in time;
therefore the world does not oppose his will;
his use of soldiers is to protect the people from calamity;
therefore the people do not resent their labor:
this is the way to maintain strength and might without losing it.
Those who lose this are in danger!"
The King of Wú angrily changed his expression,
and was displeased.
Yàn Zǐ said:
"My lord's business is finished,
I, Yīng, have no crime deserving of the axe and chisel,
I ask to take my leave and depart."
Then he was never seen again.
4.12 《Yàn Zǐ's Mission to Lǔ; The Lord of Lǔ Asks Why He Serves a Crooked Ruler; Yàn Zǐ Replies to Protect His Clan》
Yàn Zǐ was on a mission to Lǔ.
He met with Lord Zhāo.
Lord Zhāo said with pleasure:
"There are many in the world who speak to me about you, Grand Master,
now I have met you and admire what I have heard,
may I speak privately without incurring guilt?
I hear that the rulers of the great states
are indeed crooked rulers,
why do you, Grand Master,
serve a crooked ruler with your conduct?"
Yàn Zǐ hesitated and replied:
"I, Yīng, am unworthy,
The members of Ying's clan are not as good as Ying,
yet five hundred families depend on Ying to offer sacrifices to their ancestors,
therefore, Ying dares not choose a lord for himself."
Yan Zi went out,
Duke Zhao said to others:
"Yan Zi is a truly benevolent man,
he restored a fugitive lord,
stabilized a precarious state,
yet sought no personal gain;
he disgraced the corpse of Cui Zhu,
and wiped out the rebellious gang,
yet gained no fame from it;
he ensured that Qi had no worries from the feudal lords abroad,
nor troubles with the state within,
yet he does not boast of his achievements;
he is modestly unfulfilled,
and withdraws to rely on his clan.
Yan Zi can indeed be called a benevolent man."
4.13 《Duke Zhao of Lu asks Yan Zi why the whole state of Lu is confused, and Yan Zi answers that it is because it has transformed into one mind》
Yan Zi was a guest in Lu,
Duke Zhao of Lu asked him, saying:
"I have heard that,
no more than three people are confused. Now I consider it with a whole state,
Lu cannot avoid disorder, why is that?"
Yan Zi replied:
"Those whom your Lord respects, promotes and enriches,
when they enter, they work with you to plan for their own well-being,
Those who are sent out to plan for the state,
and those close to the left and right,
all share the same mind as the ruler.
Rewarding the state of Lǔ and transforming it into one mind,
there is no room for duplicity, so how could there be room for treachery?
Those who are close to the ruler's side,
and obstruct the power of the central court,
are the reason why the state is not well governed;
those who slander and flatter on the left and right,
and together block good advice,
are the reason why actions decline;
scholars who hold onto their salaries,
and travelers who cultivate connections,
are the reason why the person is in danger.
The *Book of Odes* says:
"Luxuriant are the *yu* and *pu* trees,
we use them for fuel,
dignified and numerous is the sovereign,
those on the left and right attend to him."
This says that the ancient sage kings and wise rulers employed good men.
Therefore, externally knowing the truth of matters,
and internally obtaining sincere loyalty,
one is thus not misled."
4.14《Duke Zhāo of Lǔ Asks About Pacifying the State and People, Yànzǐ Responds with Serving the Great, Nurturing the Small, Listening Carefully, and Being Frugal》
Yànzǐ was sent as an envoy to Lǔ.
Duke Zhāo of Lǔ asked, saying:
"Great Master, you have condescended to visit our humble state,
rán rǔ lín bì yì,
I greatly appreciate it.
